Malevolence means a deep, deliberate desire to cause harm or suffering to others. It is not just disliking someone — it is actively wishing bad things upon them, or taking pleasure in their pain. It describes an attitude of ill will so strong that it becomes a defining feature of someone's character or behaviour.

Think of it in two parts: the wish and the willingness.

A malevolent person does not accidentally hurt others. They want to. They derive a kind of dark satisfaction from seeing others suffer, fail, or feel pain. This makes malevolence very different from, say, carelessness or anger. Anger is usually a reaction — hot, sudden, and often temporary. Malevolence is cooler, more deliberate, and often more lasting. It is not a burst of fury; it is a settled, deep-seated orientation toward harm.

Malevolence sits at the serious end of the spectrum of negative feelings. Consider this scale:

  • Irritation → mild annoyance
  • Resentment → holding a grudge
  • Spite → wanting to hurt someone because of a personal grievance
  • Malice → a firm intention to do harm
  • Malevolence → a broader, more fundamental disposition toward evil and harm

Malevolence is not petty. When you use this word, you are describing something deep and significant — not a bad mood or a minor grudge, but a genuine, often ingrained desire for harm.
Malevolence vs. Malice — a common confusion

These two words are closely related and are often used interchangeably, but there is a useful distinction:

Malice tends to be more specific and action-oriented. It usually refers to the intention behind a particular act — "He spread the rumour with malice." It is targeted.

Malevolence is broader and more about a general state of being or an attitude. It describes a person's character or outlook rather than a single act — "There was a deep malevolence in everything she did." It colours who someone is, not just what they did once.

In short: malice is often the tool; malevolence is often the personality behind it.
What it looks like in real life

Malevolence can show itself in many ways — subtle or obvious:

  • A powerful person who enjoys watching their employees fail and does nothing to help them
  • A character in a story who manipulates others not for any personal gain, but simply because they enjoy causing misery
  • Someone who, after a falling-out, quietly works to destroy another person's reputation over years

Notice that in all these cases, the harm is intentional, often calculated, and sometimes sustained. That is the fingerprint of malevolence.

The direct antonym of malevolence is benevolence — the desire to do good for others, to help, to bring wellbeing. The two words are mirror images. Where benevolence means "wishing good," malevolence means "wishing ill."

• "The villain's eyes were filled with malevolence as he planned his revenge."
  • "She sensed a quiet malevolence behind his polite smile."
  • "The regime's malevolence toward its own citizens was undeniable."
  • "His actions were not born of ignorance — they carried real malevolence."
Malevolence is a deep, deliberate desire to cause harm or suffering to others — not out of anger or accident, but out of a genuine, often coldly felt wish for evil.
